title: the Markandeya
tomorrow: a ring with a note: open it on your worst day. what's inside?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Markandeya and the Devi Mahatmya: two betrayed men who couldn't stop caring, and a refrain that keeps bowing. The power that binds is the power that frees. Today, the same Purana, at a cradle.
screen: `THE POWER THAT BINDS IS THE POWER THAT FREES.`

segments.voice: Some nights a kid comes home from a party in tears because somebody called her a name. What do you sing to that? In the Markandeya Purana, a queen named Madalasa sings something strange at a cradle. Not the moon, not sleep, not a cow coming home. In paraphrase: child, you are pure. The name you were given was only made up for you. You are not this body, so why are you crying?
screen: `HOME FROM THE PARTY, IN TEARS.` → `A QUEEN AT A CRADLE.` → `THE NAME WAS ONLY MADE UP FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Madalasa sings the same kind of song to each of her newborn sons: you are pure, you are awake, you are free of stain. This body is made of the elements, and it isn't you. The text says her older sons grew up hearing it, and when they came of age, they didn't want the throne. They left for the forest to look for what the song told them they were. So the king, their father, asks her for something different: sing another song to the next one, so the kingdom has a king. Here's what the story is doing. A teaching about the self, the kind the Upanishads give to sages, is put in a mother's mouth at bedtime. Nobody climbs a mountain to hear it. And the Purana takes it seriously enough to show it working: children raised on those words walked out of a palace. What it gives a hard night is simple. The names people call you are real enough to sting, and they still aren't you. The song doesn't say the hurt is fake. It says the child is bigger than the name. Something a parent could say at the edge of a bed, tonight, in any language: you are more than anything anyone calls you.
screen: `YOU ARE PURE, AWAKE, FREE.` · `THE OLDER SONS LEAVE THE PALACE.` · `A SAGE'S TEACHING AT BEDTIME.` · `THE HURT IS REAL. IT ISN'T YOU.` · then, large: `MORE THAN ANY NAME.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your chest and feel it rise and fall. Let the names you carry come up one at a time, the one on your papers, the ones family uses, a few people have used unkindly, and let each one pass under your hand. Stay with whoever is breathing there before any name.
The Markandeya. The Purana told in the sage Markandeya's name, and inside it, Madalasa's lullaby to her sons.
Your line: the Markandeya. A song that tells a child she is more than any name. Day done.

howItsDone: Madalasa's lullaby, which opens 'shuddho'si buddho'si niranjano'si', is sung or recited by some Hindu families and teachers, and retold as a story about raising children with a sense of the self.

notes: 2026-10-14 recipe v3 rewrite (life shape): kept title, word, carry, source, story and most games of the 2026-10-13 draft; new hook from the listener's world (a child in tears after a party), a line for parents ('you are more than anything anyone calls you'), and Priya's storyline (her little cousin Anaya after garba). The earlier draft's note about 1515–1516 is settled: 1515 told Harishchandra and 1516 the Devi Mahatmya's frame, so Madalasa is new here.

Lullaby paraphrased, not quoted: no validator-listed public-domain translation covers the Markandeya Purana (Pargiter 1904 is public domain but not on the list). Confirm the paraphrase ('you are pure, awake, free of stain; the name is made up; the body is of the elements').
Kept the sons uncounted ('her older sons') per the claims rule; the text names three before Alarka. The sons' names are left out on purpose.

Original: शुद्धोऽसि (shuddho'si), from the lullaby's well-known opening 'shuddho'si buddho'si niranjano'si'; confirm spelling and that it fits the critical text. howItsDone repeats that opening; confirm.
The reading 'the hurt is real; it isn't you' is the script's gloss on the lullaby, labeled as what the story gives a hard night; a Keeper should confirm it doesn't flatten the teaching.
Practice kind: a body posture (hand on chest). 'The one on your papers' stays neutral about who has a passport.
